exam: A patient post‑cervical lymph node excision presents with shoulder droop – what is the most likely nerve injured and why? — Spinal accessory nerve; it innervates trapezius and is vulnerable during neck surgery.

How would you differentiate accessory nerve palsy from a rotator cuff tear at the bedside? — Test SCM and trapezius strength; rotator cuff injury shows pain on active abduction but normal neck muscle function.

What is the first investigation if a patient develops a painful neck swelling after a traditional herbal injection? — Bedside ultrasound to look for abscess compressing the nerve; if unavailable, examine for fluctuance and start empirical antibiotics.
When is surgical nerve transfer indicated in accessory nerve palsy? — When there is no functional recovery after 6‑12 months and the deficit severely limits daily activities.

Why are NSAIDs preferred over steroids in most cases of accessory nerve palsy? — NSAIDs control pain and inflammation without the systemic effects of steroids, which are only needed if an autoimmune cause is proven.

A trainee suggests ordering an MRI for every case of shoulder droop in a district hospital – how would you respond? — Emphasise clinical localisation first; MRI is reserved for unclear cases or suspected tumour, not routine.
What physiotherapy exercises should be started immediately after diagnosis? — Pendulum swings, scapular retraction, and assisted shoulder shrug to maintain range and prevent stiffness.

A patient with HIV presents with neck lymphadenitis and accessory nerve palsy – what additional cause should you consider? — Mycobacterial (TB) lymphadenitis compressing the nerve; obtain sputum or GeneXpert if possible.
ai.title: Accessory Nerve Palsy
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Weakness of shoulder elevation and head rotation due to spinal accessory nerve injury. Common after neck surgery, trauma, or infection. Recognise patterns, investigate causes, and manage promptly to prevent permanent disability.

b: SCM weakness → difficulty turning head to opposite side
Trapezius weakness → shoulder droop, winged scapula, limited abduction above 90°
sections.p: The spinal accessory nerve (cranial nerve XI) supplies the sternocleidomastoid (SCM) and trapezius muscles. Palsy presents with drooping shoulder, difficulty raising the arm above horizontal, and head rotation weakness.

b: Proximal lesion (root) → SCM and trapezius both weak
Distal lesion (after SCM branch) → isolated trapezius weakness
Look for associated neck pain, scar, or lymphadenopathy
sections.p: Identify the level of lesion (proximal vs distal) and differentiate from other shoulder girdle disorders. Consider local (surgical) and systemic (infection) causes, especially those prevalent in low‑resource settings.

b: Scapular winging may mimic long thoracic nerve injury
Delayed repair reduces chance of full recovery
sections.p: Unrecognised palsy can lead to chronic shoulder pain, scapular dyskinesis and functional limitation. Early physiotherapy improves outcomes; severe cases may need surgical nerve transfer.

t.b: Confirms pattern of weakness and localises lesion; guides further work‑up
Detects cervical lymphadenitis, abscess or mass compressing the nerve; if unavailable, rely on clinical signs and history
Shows nerve continuity, tumour, or post‑surgical fibrosis; when not available, CT or plain radiograph may reveal bony injury
Quantifies denervation and distinguishes neuropraxia from axon loss; not essential for initial management

b: Remove compressive lesion (drain abscess, excise tumour, revise surgical scar)
Analgesia with NSAIDs for pain; avoid steroids unless inflammatory cause is proven
Physiotherapy: scapular stabilisation, pendulum exercises, gradual resisted elevation
Consider nerve transfer (spinal accessory to suprascapular) for long‑standing palsy
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, protect the shoulder, and start early rehabilitation. Surgery is reserved for persistent deficits after 6‑12 months.

b: Ask patient to turn head to opposite side – SCM weakness gives limited rotation
Ask patient to shrug shoulders – trapezius weakness produces asymmetrical elevation
Observe scapular winging – lateral border prominence suggests long thoracic nerve, not accessory
sections.p: Focus on pattern of weakness, history of neck surgery or infection, and simple bedside tests that differentiate from other shoulder palsies.

b: Assuming all shoulder droop is rotator cuff pathology
Neglecting to examine SCM – missing combined weakness
Ordering expensive imaging before a clear clinical diagnosis in low‑resource settings
sections.p: Mistaking accessory palsy for rotator cuff tear or long thoracic nerve injury leads to inappropriate referrals.

whenToSeekHelp: Progressive shoulder pain with loss of arm elevation
Rapidly expanding neck swelling suggesting abscess
Neurological deterioration (e.g., new cranial nerve deficits)
